kinds.a: grand boubou · mbubb · babban riga · kulwu · dara'a · Senegalese kaftan
kinds.d: Very wide flowing West African robe worn over a tunic and drawstring trousers; the Wolof grand boubou, Yoruba agbada and Hausa babban riga are its main forms.

x.d: Wolof-named flowing wide-sleeved robe of the Sahel, usually of bazin (cotton damask) with dense embroidery, worn over a caftan and loose trousers.
x.y: adopted by 12th–13th-century Sahelian nobility; current form Senegal

v.d: Intricately embroidered boubou of French-speaking West Africa, tied to Muslim religious and wedding dress.
Mauritanian and Western Saharan boubou in white or blue bazin with gold embroidery, signalling Moorish identity.
Ankle-length pullover robe with long bell sleeves worn with matching tubay trousers and kufi; formal wear across West Africa.
Mauritanian women's boubou variant, often resist-dyed.

x.dt: bazin (cotton damask), brocade, lace, synthetics · embroidery density · colour · worn with kufi or turban

x.d: Yoruba prestige robe: a rectangular centrepiece with wide sleeves, embroidered neck and chest pockets, worn with buba or dansiki, sokoto trousers and fila cap.
x.y: adopted from Hausa/Fulani riga; documented among Yoruba by 18th century

v.d: Largest, most heavily embroidered ceremonial agbada (agbada amurode), usually in aso oke.
Casual smaller agbada (agbada iwole) in light plain cotton, named after Dr Oguntola Sapara who had his tailor cut down the robe.
Shorter-sleeved Yoruba variant sharing the agbada's embroidered hand pockets.
Agbada in etu aso oke, the indigo cotton weave striped like guinea-fowl plumage.

x.dt: aso oke (etu, sanyan, alari) · adire, brocade, damask, lace · embroidery motifs · trousers sooro or kembe · cap gobi, abetiaja or labankada

x.d: Hausa aristocratic robe of hand-woven cotton strips with silk embroidery at neck, worn with embroidered trousers, rawani turban and alkyabba cloak.
x.y: Hausa states, documented from 11th century; Kano and Zaria production

v.d: Robe with the 'two knives' motif of paired downward triangles on the front, often with spiral motifs on the back.
Several robes worn one over another by aristocracy for added prestige.

x.dt: hand-woven cotton strip cloth · silk or cotton embroidery · tan, white, indigo · Kano, Zaria workshops

kinds.d: Loose pullover West African tunic with ornate V-shaped printed or embroidered neckline, worn informally or as a suit with sokoto trousers and kufi cap.

x.a: Angelina · Miriam Makeba · Ya Mado · traditional print dashiki
x.d: The trademark dashiki: a wax/Java print with a bold embroidered-look yoke designed by Toon van de Manakker for Vlisco after 19th-century Ethiopian tunics.

v.d: Original Helmond-designed print; named 'Angelina' in Ghana after The Sweet Talks' highlife hit of the 1970s.
Congolese names for the same print, after the singer and the lyric in Fabregas's 'Mascara' video.
First US-manufactured dashiki, popularised during the Civil Rights and Black Power era.

x.dt: colourways · yoke print or embroidery · thigh, knee or ankle length · cotton, lace

kinds.a: kaba · slit and kaba · lappa suit · docket and lappa · genwu
kinds.d: Ghanaian and West African women's set: a fitted sewn blouse (kaba) with an ankle-length wrapped or sewn skirt (asetam or slit) and a matching cover cloth (nguso).
t: kaba with wrapped asetam and nguso

x.d: Blouse covering the shoulders ('cover' → kaba) with a two-yard wrapped waist cloth, later replaced by the designer-made ankle-length 'slit' skirt.
x.y: 20th century; slit developed by Ghanaian designers in the later 20th century

v.d: Original form: kaba with a wrapped two-yard asetam and a second nguso cloth used as headgear or baby carrier.
Kaba with a skirt-like ankle-length slit, easier to wear than the wrapped cloth.
Liberian name for the ensemble; called docket and lappa in Sierra Leone and genwu in Benin.
Modern kente and wax-print interpretations such as the Northern Kente dress worn by Samira Bawumia at the 2017 inauguration.

x.dt: wax print or java print · kente · lace · sleeve and neckline styles · matching headwrap

kinds.a: kemis · bahelawi kemis · Ethiopian traditional dress · Shewa Amhara dress
kinds.d: Long white hand-woven cotton (shemma) dress with woven tilet/tibeb borders at hem, sleeves and neckline, worn with a netela shawl.
t: regional variants: Shewa, Gojjam, Gondar, Wollo
bale albo kemis two-piece with embroidered trousers

x.d: Kemis with a continuous woven tibeb band encircling the hem; the most recognised silhouette, made from narrow-loom shemma strips stitched side by side.
x.y: Shewa highlands; Addis Ababa (Shiro Meda) workshops from the 1890s

v.d: 'Descending border': vertical tilet panel from chest to hem, used for formal wear.
'Half border': pattern restricted to the lower back, for daily wear.
Finer, softer shemma developed at Shiro Meda for the court and named after Empress Menen Asfaw.
Cabin-crew uniform in white menen shemma with tilet and tibeb borders that spread the style internationally.

x.dt: shemma fetel, menen or saba · tibeb colours (green, red jano) · tilf hand embroidery · length · with netela

kinds.a: thobe · tobe · tob · tiyyab · melhfa · lafaya
kinds.d: Sudanese women's seamless outer wrap, a rectangle about 2 m wide and 4–7 m long draped over a dress and around the head.

x.d: Seamless 4–7 m wrap worn by Sudanese women since Nubian and Kushite times, replacing the rahat skirt and marking marital status and social role.
x.y: ancient Nile Valley roots; worn by unmarried girls only from the 1950s

v.d: Plain white wrap of teachers, nurses and professional women, symbol of education and civic duty.
Indigo-dyed Nubian toub of northern Sudan, historically coarse and a marker of status.
Mauritanian and Western Saharan form of the wrap (also dampé in Mali).
Form worn in northern Nigeria, Niger and Chad.

x.dt: length 4–7 m × 2 m · cotton, silk, synthetics · embroidery · colour · drape style

kinds.a: Herero dress · ohorokova · shweshwe dress · seshoeshoe dress
kinds.d: Southern African women's dresses of colonial-era cut in local cloth: the Herero floor-length ohorokova with horned headdress and Basotho dresses in printed shweshwe cotton.
t: Herero ohorokova gown with otjikaiva horned headdress
shweshwe (seshoeshoe) dress, Basotho and makoti styles

x.d: Full-length, voluminous Victorian-derived gown of Herero women with layered petticoats and the cow-horn otjikaiva headdress, worn as a marker of identity and memory of the Herero genocide.

v.d: Floor-length skirt, long sleeves and wide horned otjikaiva.
Windhoek designer's reinterpretation with extra petticoats, sleeveless cuts and slimmer stylised headdress.

x.dt: fabric print · petticoat layers · sleeve · headdress width

brands.d: Helmond-based designer and maker of African wax prints for West and Central Africa; group brands Vlisco, Woodin, Uniwax and GTP.
eras: Toon van de Manakker, textile designer, 1962 Angelina

brands.d: Accra fashion house founded by Aisha Ayensu and named after her seamstress grandmother; modern Ghanaian womenswear.
eras: Aisha Ayensu, founder and creative director, 2008–

brands.d: Accra brand of Kabutey and Sumaiya Dzietror known for hand-beaded bridal gowns and kente and wax-print dresses, including Samira Bawumia's 2017 Northern Kente dress.
US wholesaler of dashikis, African print clothing and accessories sold under its own name.
Windhoek Herero designer modernising the ohorokova dress and otjikaiva headdress for younger wearers.

traditions.d: Horizontal-loom strip weave sewn into broad cloth for agbada and other prestige dress.
traditions.tech: narrow-band weaving on horizontal loom, strips 4–6 in wide sewn edge to edge
traditions.mat: cotton, wild silk; indigo and red dyes
traditions.auth: strip seams visible; named weaves alari (red silk), sanyan (beige silk), etu (indigo cotton)

traditions.d: Hand-embroidered geometric motifs on strip-woven babban riga robes of the Hausa aristocracy.
traditions.tech: hand embroidery in silk or cotton on stitched cotton panels
traditions.auth: aska biyu 'two knives' triangles on front left, spiral motifs at back; strip-cloth construction

traditions.r: Amhara highlands and Shiro Meda, Addis Ababa, Ethiopia
traditions.p: Solomonic era to present; Shiro Meda workshops from the 1890s
traditions.d: Narrow-loom hand-spun cotton cloth with woven tilet and tibeb borders, the base of the Habesha kemis and netela.
traditions.tech: women hand-spin, men weave long strips on narrow looms; borders woven in on the loom, tilf embroidery added after
traditions.mat: hand-spun cotton; silk or rayon in saba
ctr: Shiro Meda, Addis Ababa (Gudnesh site, 650+ weavers)
traditions.auth: strips stitched side by side; tibeb woven not printed; fabric grades fetel, menen, saba

notes: Rebuilt the African dress shelf from one old kind (Boubou, 1 model) into six kinds with 9 archetypes. Old model 'Agbada' became an archetype under Boubou & agbada; old source (taecouture.net) replaced by retrieved Wikipedia/museum pages. Added 'Southern African dress' (Herero ohorokova + shweshwe dress) as a kind rather than a loose note because no planned kind could hold it; shweshwe cloth itself stays with Named cloths. Left out: Sudanese toub brands Sara Issa and Toob for Less (no page about them could be retrieved this session, so no brand entries); Africa Imports kept only as a light range list and stub because it is a wholesaler. Shiro Meda appears as a tradition centre (Shemma weaving) rather than a brand. The wiki tool failed mid-session (lock error), so Wikipedia pages were fetched directly; Vlisco and Seshoeshoe pages were confirmed via the first wiki call. Version years and names are only those stated on retrieved pages; vague eras used where sources give none.
